p.src: Good notation is not decoration. In a subject built from abstract vectors and complex numbers, a notation that lets us move symbols without repeatedly translating them into words is part of the machinery. Dirac’s bra–ket notation is valuable for precisely this reason: it keeps the geometry of the state space visible while allowing us to calculate with components and matrices.

p.src: Our immediate task is mathematical. We shall introduce linear operators, learn how they act on bras as well as kets, and isolate the special class called Hermitian operators. Only then shall we attach the physical words observable, measurement result, and probability. The reward is that the three spin observables emerge as the Pauli matrices rather than being handed to us as objects to memorize.

p.src: Orthonormal Bases and Components

u.src: Orthonormal Bases and Components
en: Orthonormal Bases and Components

p.src: The states form a complex linear vector space. Its ket vectors can be added and multiplied by complex numbers. Associated with every ket $\ket{A}$ is a bra $\bra{A}$, obtained by the conjugate-dual operation. A basis is not unique, but once one has been chosen every vector can be described by its components in that basis.

p.src: Let $\bigl\{\ket{1},\ket{2},\ldots,\ket{N}\bigr\}$ be an orthonormal basis. Orthogonality and normalization are summarized by $\braket{j}{i}=\delta_{ji}.$ Here $\delta_{ji}$ is one when $j=i$ and zero otherwise. The dimension $N$ is the maximum number of mutually orthogonal directions in the space; a complete orthonormal basis contains exactly that many vectors.

p.src: Substitution of Equation  back into Equation  gives the especially useful form $\ket{A}=\sum_i\ket{i}\braket{i}{A}.$ The sum has done nothing to the vector; it has only resolved the vector into its basis directions and then rebuilt it. We shall use this operation repeatedly. It is usually described as inserting a complete set of states, because $\sum_i\ket{i}\bra{i}=\mathbf 1.$

p.src: Linear Operators as Machines

u.src: Linear Operators as Machines
en: Linear Operators as Machines

p.src: A linear operator $M$ is a rule that takes an input ket to a unique output ket. A useful picture, due to John Wheeler, is a machine with an input port and an output port: insert $\ket{A}$, turn the wheel, and receive $M\ket{A}$. The output is fixed by the input. The reverse need not be unique; two inputs may produce the same output, and an inverse machine need not exist.

The reverse need not be unique; two inputs may produce the same output, and an inverse machine need not exist.

p.src:
The adjective linear consists of two rules. For a complex number $z$, $\begin{aligned}
M\bigl(z\ket{A}\bigr)&=z\,M\ket{A}, \\
M\bigl(\ket{A}+\ket{B}\bigr)&=M\ket{A}+M\ket{B}.
\end{aligned}$ A scalar passes through the machine unchanged, and a sum may be processed one term at a time. These rules also imply linearity for any finite complex linear combination.

p.src: From an Operator to Its Matrix

u.src: From an Operator to Its Matrix
en: From an Operator to Its Matrix

p.src:
Suppose the machine sends $\ket{A}$ to $\ket{B}$: $M\ket{A}=\ket{B}.$ Choose the same orthonormal basis for input and output and write $\ket{A}=\sum_j\alpha_j\ket{j},
\qquad
\ket{B}=\sum_i\beta_i\ket{i}.$ To find the $i$-th output component, project Equation  with $\bra{i}$: $\bra{i}M\ket{A}=\braket{i}{B}=\beta_i.$ Now insert the expansion of $\ket{A}$: $\begin{aligned}
\bra{i}M\ket{A}
 &=\sum_j\bra{i}M\ket{j}\braket{j}{A}\\
 &=\sum_j\bra{i}M\ket{j}\alpha_j
 =\beta_i.\end{aligned}$ The numbers $m_{ij}\equiv\bra{i}M\ket{j}$ are the matrix elements of $M$ in the chosen basis. Consequently, $\boxed{\sum_jm_{ij}\alpha_j=\beta_i.}$

p.src: Bras, Kets, and Anti-Linearity

u.src: Bras, Kets, and Anti-Linearity
en: Bras, Kets, and Anti-Linearity

p.src: Multiplication by a fixed complex number is a simple linear operator. Complex conjugation is not. If $K$ denotes conjugation, then $K\bigl(z\ket{A}\bigr)=z^*K\ket{A},$ not $zK\ket{A}$. Such a map is called anti-linear. The name does not mean the opposite of linear; it records the conjugation of scalars. Its deeper relation to antiparticles lies beyond the present discussion.

=

\equiv
\bra{A}M\ket{B}.$

p.src:
To see why this is possible, expand both vectors: $\begin{aligned}
\bra{A}M\ket{B}
 &=\left(\sum_i\alpha_i^*\bra{i}\right)
   M
   \left(\sum_j\beta_j\ket{j}\right)\\
 &=\sum_{ij}\alpha_i^*m_{ij}\beta_j.
\end{aligned}$ This is an ordinary double sum. We may sum over $j$ first and regard $M$ as acting on the ket, or sum over $i$ first and regard it as acting on the bra. The answer is the same. The notation was arranged this way precisely so that unnecessary brackets can be removed.

p.src: There is a second and different bra-side question. Suppose $M\ket{A}=\ket{B}.$ What operator turns the corresponding bra $\bra{A}$ into $\bra{B}$? It is not generally $M$ itself. If $M$ were multiplication by a complex number $z$, the ket equation would be $\ket{B}=z\ket{A}$, while the bra equation would be $\bra{B}=z^*\bra{A}$.

p.src: A general operator changes the direction of a vector. A rotation in ordinary three-dimensional space, for example, turns almost every vector away from itself. The rotation axis is exceptional: a vector along that axis returns in the same direction. This is the model for an eigenvector.

p.src: A nontrivial rotation of a real two-dimensional plane illustrates the opposite possibility: there is no real direction left fixed up to a real scale. Thus a generic operator on a restricted real space need not have a real eigenvector. The Hermitian operators on the complex state spaces used in quantum mechanics have much stronger properties.

p.src: Different Eigenvalues Give Orthogonal Eigenvectors

p.src:
Let $M\ket{i}=\lambda_i\ket{i},
\qquad
M\ket{j}=\lambda_j\ket{j},$ where $M$ is Hermitian. Dagger the second equation. Its eigenvalue is already known to be real: $\bra{j}M=\lambda_j\bra{j}.$ Now multiply the first equation by $\bra{j}$ and the bra equation by $\ket{i}$: $\begin{aligned}
\bra{j}M\ket{i}&=\lambda_i\braket{j}{i},\\
\bra{j}M\ket{i}&=\lambda_j\braket{j}{i}.\end{aligned}$ Subtracting gives $\boxed{(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)\braket{j}{i}=0.}$ If $\lambda_i\ne\lambda_j$, then $\braket{j}{i}=0.$ The eigendirections are orthogonal.

p.src: Orthogonality also has a physical reading. Two orthogonal states can be distinguished without ambiguity by a suitable measurement. Eigenstates with different eigenvalues must be distinguishable because the apparatus reports different real numbers for them. The algebra and the operational meaning are already pointing to the same correspondence.

The algebra and the operational meaning are already pointing to the same correspondence.

p.src: We now have enough formalism to state the basic quantum-mechanical correspondences. They may sound foreign when first encountered. Their meaning becomes concrete only after they are used, so let us state them cleanly and then return at once to the spin experiment.

p.src: A single measurement produces a real number. One may package two compatible real readings into a complex number, but that package still contains two measurements. The elementary output of one detector is real. Hermitian operators are therefore the natural candidates: their eigenvalues are real, and their eigenvectors form a complete orthonormal basis.

p.src:

=\left|\braket{i}{A}\right|^2
=\braket{i}{A}\braket{A}{i}.$

p.src: Normalization and Completeness

u.src: Normalization and Completeness
en: Normalization and Completeness

p.src:
The probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes must add to one: $\sum_i\left|\braket{i}{A}\right|^2=1.$ Insert the complete eigenbasis: $\begin{aligned}
\sum_i\left|\braket{i}{A}\right|^2
 &=\sum_i\braket{A}{i}\braket{i}{A}\\
 &=\bra{A}\left(\sum_i\ket{i}\bra{i}\right)\ket{A}\\
 &=\braket{A}{A}.\end{aligned}$ Hence an allowable state vector is normalized, $\braket{A}{A}=1.$ If $\ket{A}=\sum_i\alpha_i\ket{i}$, the same condition is $\sum_i\alpha_i^*\alpha_i=1.$ This is one real constraint on the complex components.

p.src: There is another redundancy. Multiplying every component by the same phase, $\ket{A}\longmapsto e^{i\theta}\ket{A},$ multiplies every amplitude by $e^{i\theta}$ and leaves every squared magnitude unchanged. No measurement can detect that common phase. Relative phases between components remain physical; only a phase multiplying the whole state is redundant.

p.src: Thus two real parameters in an arbitrary complex vector do not specify the physical state: its magnitude is fixed by normalization, and its overall phase is unobservable. This is the same parameter count encountered for a single spin, now derived from the general probability rule.

p.src:
Choose the up–down basis. Definite $z$-spin means $\sigma_z\ket{u}=+\ket{u},
\qquad
\sigma_z\ket{d}=-\ket{d}.$ The two eigenvalues are different, so Hermiticity implies $\braket{u}{d}=0$.

u.src:
Choose the up–down basis. Definite $z$-spin means $\sigma_z\ket{u}=+\ket{u},
\qquad
\sigma_z\ket{d}=-\ket{d}.$ The two eigenvalues are different, so Hermiticity implies $\braket{u}{d}=0$.
en:
Choose the up–down basis. Definite $z$-spin means $\sigma_z\ket{u}=+\ket{u},
\qquad
\sigma_z\ket{d}=-\ket{d}.$ The two eigenvalues are different, so Hermiticity implies $\braket{u}{d}=0$.

p.src:
Compute the four matrix elements: $\begin{aligned}
\bra{u}\sigma_z\ket{u}&=+1,&
\bra{u}\sigma_z\ket{d}&=-\braket{u}{d}=0,\\
\bra{d}\sigma_z\ket{u}&=\braket{d}{u}=0,&
\bra{d}\sigma_z\ket{d}&=-1.\end{aligned}$ Therefore $\boxed{
\sigma_z=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&-1
\end{pmatrix}_{\{u,d\}}.}$ The coordinate columns are $\ket{u}\widehat{=}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\ket{d}\widehat{=}\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$ Multiplication by Equation  returns the first column unchanged and the second with a minus sign, exactly as the eigenvalue equations require.

p.src:
In the right–left basis, $\sigma_x$ would have the same diagonal form. That would be easy but uninformative. Keep the up–down basis and use $\sigma_x\ket{r}=+\ket{r},
\qquad
\sigma_x\ket{l}=-\ket{l}.$ The two bases are related by $\begin{aligned}
\ket{r}&=\frac{\ket{u}+\ket{d}}{\sqrt2},&
\ket{l}&=\frac{\ket{u}-\ket{d}}{\sqrt2},\\
\ket{u}&=\frac{\ket{r}+\ket{l}}{\sqrt2},&
\ket{d}&=\frac{\ket{r}-\ket{l}}{\sqrt2}.
\end{aligned}$

p.src:
We have obtained $\begin{aligned}
\sigma_x&=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\\[0.4em]
\sigma_y&=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\\[0.4em]
\sigma_z&=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$ They are Hermitian, have eigenvalues $\pm1$, and possess exactly the definite-spin eigenvectors demanded by the analyzer experiments.
